payload.title: Block on a table connected to a hanging block

stimulus.description: A block of mass $m_1=3\text{ kg}$ rests on a horizontal table. payload.title: Block-spring oscillator: energy, graph and prediction

stimulus.description: A block of mass $m=1\text{ kg}$ is attached to a horizontal spring of spring constant $k=50\text{ N/m}$ on a frictionless surface. The block is pulled to a position $x=+A$ with $A=0.2\text{ m}$ and released from rest at $t=0$.

parts.model_answer: At $+A$: $U_s=E$, $K=0$. At $0$: $K=E$, $U_s=0$. At $-A/2$: $U_s=E/4$, $K=3E/4$. Total $E=\tfrac12kA^2=1.0000\text{ J}$ in every state.

common_errors: splits the energy equally

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed of the block as it passes $x=0$ in terms of $m$, $k$, and $A$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Sets the initial spring energy equal to the kinetic energy at the equilibrium position: $\tfrac12kA^2=\tfrac12mv^2$
common_errors: uses kA = mv

rubric_rows.criterion: Solves for $v=A\sqrt{k/m}$
common_errors: omits the square root

parts.label: C

parts.model_answer: A cosine curve starting at $+A=0.2\text{ m}$ with period $P=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}\approx 0.89\text{ s}$, repeated twice.

common_errors: starts at zero like a sine

payload.title: Claim about kinetic energy in a perfectly inelastic collision

stimulus.description: A cart of mass $m$ moving at speed $v_0=4\text{ m/s}$ on a frictionless track collides with a stationary cart of mass $3m$. The carts stick together. A student claims that the kinetic energy of the two-cart system is the same before and after the collision.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Do you agree or disagree with the student's claim? Justify your answer qualitatively without calculating numbers.
parts.model_answer: Disagree. Momentum is conserved because there is no net external horizontal force, but the carts stick together (a perfectly inelastic collision) so some kinetic energy is transformed into internal energy.

rubric_rows.criterion: Disagrees with the claim (kinetic energy is not conserved)
common_errors: agrees because momentum is conserved

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies the claim by distinguishing that momentum is conserved (no net external force) from kinetic energy, which is not
common_errors: says both are conserved in every collision

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains that sticking together transforms kinetic energy into internal energy (or notes the carts do not separate)
common_errors: attributes the loss to friction with the track

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed $v_f$ of the combined carts in terms of $v_0$ and numerical constants, and find the fraction of the initial kinetic energy that remains.
parts.model_answer: $mv_0=(m+3m)v_f$ so $v_f=v_0/4=1.000\text{ m/s}$; the remaining kinetic energy fraction is $\dfrac{(m+3m)v_f^2}{mv_0^2}=\dfrac{1}{4}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies conservation of momentum: $mv_0=(m+3m)v_f$
common_errors: adds the speeds

rubric_rows.criterion: Solves for $v_f=v_0/4$
common_errors: divides by n rather than n+1

rubric_rows.criterion: Finds the kinetic energy fraction $1/4$
common_errors: uses the speed fraction as the energy fraction

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: The stationary cart is replaced by one with a mass of $6m$ and the carts again stick together. Predict whether the fraction of the initial kinetic energy that is lost increases, decreases, or stays the same, and justify your prediction.
parts.model_answer: The fraction lost increases. The remaining fraction is $m/(m+M)$, which gets smaller as $M$ grows, so the lost fraction $M/(m+M)$ grows.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the fraction of kinetic energy lost increases
common_errors: states the lost fraction decreases for a heavier target

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with the remaining fraction $m/(m+M)$ decreasing as $M$ increases
common_errors: argues only that more mass means more energy

difficulty.label: exam_prep
difficulty.rationale: Three-part FRQ-style item within Unit 4 scope. It requires choosing momentum conservation over energy conservation for a perfectly inelastic collision, a short symbolic derivation (v_f = v0/4 and KE fraction 1/4), and a proportional-reasoning prediction (the fraction of KE lost rises from 3/4 to 6/7 as the target mass increases). Arithmetic is minimal, the wording is unambiguous, and the context is brief, so the difficulty comes only from concept application and argumentation, as is typical for a full mock exam.
